content.text: 🤿 Reading Practice
🔁 Review

In our previous lesson, we explored archaic pronouns in English. We examined forms like "thou," "thee," "thy," and "thine," their modern equivalents, and their usage in historical texts, poetry, and religious writings.
Quick Practice:
What is the modern equivalent of "thou" in this sentence: "Thou art the master of thy fate"?
Rewrite this modern sentence using archaic pronouns: "You should follow your dreams."
What social distinction did "thou" versus "you" originally convey in Early Modern English?
🎯 Overview

Reading comprehension is a fundamental skill for advanced English learners. It involves not just understanding individual words and sentences, but also grasping main ideas, identifying key details, recognizing tone and purpose, making inferences, and critically evaluating texts.

Effective reading in English requires various sub-skills: skimming for general meaning, scanning for specific information, understanding vocabulary in context, recognizing text organization, and interpreting implicit information. These skills must be practiced with different text types and genres to develop versatile reading abilities.

We read for different purposes—for information, entertainment, instruction, or analysis—and each purpose requires different approaches. At the C1 level, you should be able to understand complex, specialized texts with implicit meanings, idiomatic expressions, and cultural references, even when the subject matter isn't familiar.
🏊 Can you do?
Skim this paragraph and identify the main topic in 10 seconds:

The global transition to renewable energy sources has accelerated in recent years, driven by technological advancements, decreasing costs, and growing environmental concerns. Solar and wind power, once considered supplementary energy sources, are increasingly becoming primary contributors to national power grids. However, challenges remain in energy storage, grid infrastructure, and policy frameworks. Despite these obstacles, the momentum behind clean energy appears irreversible as countries worldwide commit to ambitious carbon reduction targets.
Scan this text and find the specific information requested below:

The exhibition will run from September 15th to December 3rd, 2025, at the National Gallery. Opening hours are Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 AM to 6:00 PM, with extended hours until 9:00 PM on Thursdays. Admission is $22 for adults, $18 for seniors, and free for children under 12 and museum members. Guided tours are available daily at 11:30 AM and 2:30 PM at no additional cost. Photography is permitted without flash. The museum café will offer special themed menus inspired by the exhibition. For more information or to purchase tickets in advance, visit
www.nationalgallery.org/specialexhibition
a. What are the opening hours on Thursday? b. How much does admission cost for a 10-year-old child? c. When are guided tours available?
Read this passage and answer the inference questions:

Mark glanced at his watch for the fifth time in as many minutes. The café was bustling with the usual lunchtime crowd, but the chair across from him remained empty. He sighed, scrolling through his messages again to confirm the time and place. No new texts had arrived. Outside, rain began to tap against the windows, matching his darkening mood. He caught the waitress's eye and reluctantly ordered a coffee. As he stirred in the sugar, he made a mental note to update his dating profile.
a. Why is Mark at the café? b. How does Mark feel? c. What can we infer about the person Mark is waiting for?
Identify the tone and purpose of this text:

URGENT NOTICE: All residents MUST evacuate the building immediately. A gas leak has been detected on the ground floor. Do NOT use elevators. Do NOT stop to collect personal belongings. Proceed to the nearest emergency exit and follow the instructions of safety personnel. This is NOT a drill.
a. What is the tone of this text? b. What is the primary purpose of this text?
🔍 Deep Dive
Reading effectively in English requires mastering various strategies and understanding different text types. Let's explore these aspects in detail to enhance your reading comprehension skills.
Reading Strategies for Different Purposes
1. Skimming
Skimming involves quickly reading a text to get the general idea or main points without focusing on details.
When to use it:
To decide if a text is relevant to your needs
To get an overview before detailed reading
When you have limited time
How to skim effectively:
Read the title, headings, and subheadings
Focus on the first and last paragraphs
Look at any images, charts, or highlighted information
Read the first sentence of each paragraph
Move your eyes quickly through the text, looking for key words
Example exercise: Skim this article about climate change and identify three main points in 30 seconds.
2. Scanning
Scanning involves quickly searching for specific information without reading the entire text.
When to use it:
To find particular facts, figures, or names
To locate answers to specific questions
When you need particular information from a longer text
How to scan effectively:
Know exactly what you're looking for
Use headings, bullet points, and formatting as guides
Look for numbers, dates, names, or key terms
Move your eyes vertically down the page rather than reading horizontally
Use Ctrl+F when reading digital texts
Example exercise: Scan a train timetable to find the departure time for a specific destination.
3. Intensive Reading
Intensive reading involves careful, detailed reading to fully understand a text.
When to use it:
For complex or important information
When studying academic material
When analyzing literature or poetry
For contracts or legal documents
How to read intensively:
Read slowly and carefully
Look up unfamiliar vocabulary
Take notes or highlight key points
Reread difficult sections
Ask questions about the content
Example exercise: Read a complex paragraph about quantum physics and explain the main concept in your own words.
4. Extensive Reading
Extensive reading involves reading widely for pleasure and general language improvement.
When to use it:
To build vocabulary naturally
To improve reading fluency
To enjoy literature in English
How to read extensively:
Choose materials slightly below your current level
Read without stopping for every unknown word
Focus on overall meaning rather than details
Read regularly for sustained periods
Example exercise: Choose an English novel that interests you and read a chapter each day for a month.
5. Critical Reading
Critical reading involves evaluating and analyzing a text rather than just understanding it.
When to use it:
When assessing the validity of arguments
When comparing different viewpoints
When researching academic topics
When analyzing media reports
How to read critically:
Identify the author's purpose and potential biases
Distinguish between facts and opinions
Evaluate the evidence presented
Consider what information might be missing
Compare with other sources on the same topic
Example exercise: Read two newspaper articles about the same political event from publications with different political leanings and analyze their differences.
Common Text Types and Their Features
1. Narrative Texts
Stories that entertain or inform through a sequence of events.
Features:
Characters, setting, plot, conflict, resolution
Chronological sequence (though not always linear)
Descriptive language and dialogue
Often uses past tense
May have themes or morals
Examples: novels, short stories, biographies, anecdotes, news stories
Reading approach:
Follow the plot development
Pay attention to character motivations
Look for themes and symbolism
Consider the narrator's perspective (first-person, third-person, etc.)
2. Descriptive Texts
Texts that create a vivid image of a person, place, object, or experience.
Features:
Sensory details (sight, sound, smell, taste, touch)
Figurative language (metaphors, similes)
Precise vocabulary
Spatial organization (top to bottom, near to far, etc.)
Examples: travel writing, nature descriptions, character portraits, product descriptions
Reading approach:
Visualize what's being described
Note the sensory details used
Identify the mood or atmosphere created
Consider why certain details were included
3. Expository Texts
Texts that explain or inform about a topic.
Features:
Clear organization (often with headings)
Facts, statistics, examples
Objective tone
Technical vocabulary
Visual aids (charts, diagrams, etc.)
Examples: textbooks, encyclopedias, how-to guides, scientific articles
Reading approach:
Identify the main ideas and supporting details
Pay attention to the organizational structure
Look for definitions of technical terms
Study any visual aids carefully
4. Argumentative Texts
Texts that present a viewpoint and attempt to persuade the reader.
Features:
Clear thesis or position
Supporting evidence and reasoning
Counterarguments and rebuttals
Persuasive language
Call to action
Examples: editorials, opinion pieces, academic essays, political speeches
Reading approach:
Identify the main argument or thesis
Evaluate the evidence presented
Recognize emotional appeals versus logical reasoning
Look for counterarguments and how they're addressed
Consider your own position on the issue
5. Instructional Texts
Texts that guide the reader through a process or procedure.
Features:
Sequential steps
Imperative verbs (commands)
Precise measurements or timings
Visual aids or diagrams
Warnings or tips
Examples: recipes, manuals, DIY guides, safety instructions
Reading approach:
Follow the sequence carefully
Pay attention to specific measurements or requirements
Note any warnings or precautions
Visualize the process before attempting it
Common Challenges for Brazilian Readers
1. False Cognates and False Friends
Words that look similar to Portuguese words but have different meanings.
Examples:
"Actually" (na verdade) vs. "atualmente" (currently)
"Attend" (comparecer) vs. "atender" (to assist/serve)
"Exquisite" (requintado) vs. "esquisito" (weird)
"Pretend" (fingir) vs. "pretender" (to intend)
"Resume" (currículo/retomar) vs. "resumir" (to summarize)
Strategy:
Create a personal list of false friends you encounter
Check the context carefully when you see a word that looks familiar
When in doubt, look up the word rather than assuming its meaning
2. Phrasal Verbs and Idiomatic Expressions
Multi-word verbs and expressions that can't be understood from their individual words.
Examples:
"To look up to someone" (admirar alguém)
"To run into someone" (encontrar alguém por acaso)
"To hit the books" (estudar intensamente)
"Under the weather" (sentindo-se mal)
"To cost an arm and a leg" (ser muito caro)
Strategy:
Pay attention to the context for clues to meaning
Learn phrasal verbs in groups by common verbs (get, put, take, etc.)
Practice with authentic materials where these expressions appear naturally
3. Complex Sentence Structures
Long sentences with multiple clauses, particularly in academic or literary texts.
Examples:
Sentences with multiple subordinate clauses
Inverted sentence structures
Sentences with parenthetical information
Complex passive constructions
Strategy:
Break down long sentences into smaller parts
Identify the main subject and verb first
Recognize linking words that show relationships between ideas
Practice reading academic texts regularly
4. Cultural References
References to history, pop culture, or traditions that may be unfamiliar.
Examples:
Historical events specific to English-speaking countries
References to TV shows, movies, or celebrities
Sports metaphors (baseball, American football)
Holidays and traditions
Strategy:
Build background knowledge through media consumption
Don't hesitate to research unfamiliar references
Read with cultural context in mind
Discuss cultural differences with native speakers when possible
5. Text Organization Differences
Different expectations for how information should be presented.
Examples:
Academic writing in English often states the main point first, then provides support
Business communications may be more direct than in Brazilian Portuguese
Different conventions for formal letters or emails
Strategy:
Familiarize yourself with genre conventions in English
Pay attention to topic sentences and concluding sentences
Look for signposting language that indicates text structure
Reading Comprehension Techniques
1. Predicting Content
Making educated guesses about what a text will contain before and during reading.
How to practice:
Look at titles, headings, images before reading
Based on the first paragraph, predict what will come next
Use your background knowledge about the topic
Confirm or adjust your predictions as you read
2. Identifying Main Ideas and Supporting Details
Distinguishing between central points and information that elaborates on them.
How to practice:
Try to summarize paragraphs in one sentence
Look for topic sentences (often at the beginning of paragraphs)
Distinguish between examples, statistics, and main arguments
Create outlines of texts you read
3. Making Inferences
Reading "between the lines" to understand implied meanings.
How to practice:
Ask yourself what the author is suggesting but not stating directly
Look for clues in word choice, tone, and context
Consider what background knowledge the author assumes
Practice with short stories where not everything is explicit
4. Recognizing Author's Purpose and Tone
Understanding why a text was written and the author's attitude toward the subject.
How to practice:
Identify if the purpose is to inform, persuade, entertain, or instruct
Note emotional or evaluative language
Consider the publication source and intended audience
Look for bias or particular perspectives
5. Summarizing and Synthesizing
Condensing information and combining ideas from different parts of a text.
How to practice:
After reading, write a one-paragraph summary
Identify connections between different sections
Compare information from multiple sources on the same topic
Explain the text to someone else in your own words
Mini Dialogues:
Situation: English Literature Class
Professor: Today we'll analyze how the author uses setting to create atmosphere in this passage. What techniques do you notice?
Student: I see a lot of sensory details, especially about the weather and lighting. The description of the "oppressive fog" seems to foreshadow something negative.
Professor: Excellent observation. The setting often mirrors the protagonist's emotional state. What else can we infer about the character from these descriptions?
Situation: Business English Course
Teacher: When reading business reports in English, what strategies help you locate key information quickly?

Student: I usually look for headings, bold text, and executive summaries first. I've noticed that in English reports, the main conclusions are often stated at the beginning, unlike in Portuguese where they might come at the end.
Teacher: That's a crucial difference. English business writing tends to be more direct, with the "bottom line" presented early. This "inverted pyramid" structure is something to watch for.
Situation: Reading Group
Facilitator: What challenges did you face while reading this chapter?

Participant: I struggled with some of the idiomatic expressions. For example, when the character said she was "feeling under the weather," I initially translated it literally before realizing it means she was feeling sick.
Facilitator: That's a common issue. Idioms rarely translate directly. Did anyone else notice expressions that might confuse Brazilian readers?
Common Errors and Formal Variations:
Translating idioms literally: "It's raining cats and dogs" ❌ → Understanding it means "It's raining heavily" ✓
Assuming cognates always have the same meaning: "I am embarrassed" ≠ "Eu estou embaraçado" (I am pregnant) ❌
Missing cultural references: Not recognizing references to American history or British literature ❌ → Researching unfamiliar references ✓
Reading word by word rather than in meaningful chunks ❌ → Reading groups of words for better comprehension and speed ✓
Academic reading requires more attention to structure and argument than casual reading
News articles in English often use more complex verb forms than their Portuguese counterparts
Business communications in English tend to be more direct and concise than in Brazilian Portuguese
Literary texts in English may contain more cultural allusions that require background knowledge
📖 Reading Practice
In this section, we'll practice with three different text types at varying levels of difficulty. For each text, we'll focus on different reading skills.
Text 1: Narrative (Intermediate)
The Unexpected Guest

Sarah had just settled down with a cup of tea when she heard a knock at the door. She wasn't expecting anyone, and the clock on the mantelpiece showed it was already past nine in the evening. Reluctantly, she put down her book and went to answer it.

Through the peephole, she could see a man in a delivery uniform, holding a package. Strange time for a delivery, she thought, but perhaps it was something important. She opened the door, keeping the security chain in place.
"Delivery for Ms. Williams," the man said cheerfully.
"That's me," Sarah replied, "but I didn't order anything."
The man consulted his clipboard. "It says here it's from a James Cooper. There's a note too."
Sarah's heart skipped a beat. James was her brother who had moved to Australia five years ago. They hadn't spoken in months due to a silly argument she could barely remember now.

She closed the door, removed the chain, and opened it again. As she signed for the package, she noticed it was postmarked from Sydney. Back in her living room, she carefully unwrapped it to find a beautiful photo album. Inside was a handwritten note: "Some memories are too precious to lose over forgotten words. I miss you, sis."

Tears welled in her eyes as she flipped through photos of their childhood, family holidays, and shared milestones. The last page held two plane tickets to Sydney and another note: "Your turn to visit. Bring Mom."
Sarah reached for her phone, no longer concerned about the late hour in Australia. Some calls couldn't wait.
Comprehension Questions:
Why was Sarah surprised by the knock at the door?
What was Sarah's relationship with James, and what had happened between them?
What did the package contain, and what was its purpose?
What can you infer about Sarah's character from her actions?
What is the theme of this short story?
Text 2: Expository (Upper Intermediate)
The Surprising Science of Decision Fatigue

Why does a judge's ruling depend partly on when the case is heard? Why do we splurge on expensive electronics we don't need? The answer lies in a phenomenon called decision fatigue—the psychological principle that explains why making decisions becomes progressively harder throughout the day.

Unlike physical fatigue, decision fatigue isn't always apparent. You don't necessarily feel tired, but your brain's ability to make high-quality decisions deteriorates after multiple decisions. This cognitive depletion affects everyone from CEOs to parents, judges to consumers.

Research from Columbia University demonstrated this effect by analyzing over 1,100 parole decisions made by judges. Prisoners who appeared early in the morning received parole about 70% of the time, while those who appeared late in the day were paroled less than 10% of the time, regardless of the crime committed. The judges, mentally depleted after making numerous decisions, defaulted to the safer option—keeping prisoners incarcerated.

Similarly, consumers face decision fatigue when shopping. After deciding between multiple products, features, and prices, our self-control weakens. This explains why supermarkets place impulse purchase items near checkout counters—by then, shoppers have depleted their decision-making resources.

The implications extend beyond shopping and legal decisions. Medical professionals make thousands of decisions daily, with studies showing that prescription rates for unnecessary antibiotics increase significantly during later appointment slots. In business, important meetings scheduled late in the day often result in status quo decisions rather than innovative solutions.

How can we combat decision fatigue? Experts recommend several strategies. First, make important decisions earlier in the day when your mental energy is highest. Second, establish routines for recurring decisions—what to wear, what to eat for breakfast—to preserve mental resources for more significant choices. Third, limit your options; while choice seems beneficial, too many alternatives can be paralyzing. Finally, take breaks between important decisions to allow your brain to recharge.

Understanding decision fatigue doesn't just explain puzzling behaviors—it provides a framework for optimizing our decision-making processes and improving outcomes in both professional and personal contexts.
Comprehension Questions:
What is decision fatigue, and how does it differ from physical fatigue?
What did the Columbia University research reveal about judges' decisions?
Why do supermarkets place impulse purchase items near checkout counters?
What are two strategies mentioned for combating decision fatigue?
How might understanding decision fatigue improve professional outcomes?
Text 3: Argumentative (Advanced)
The Digital Paradox: Is Technology Enhancing or Diminishing Democracy?

The digital revolution promised to democratize information and empower citizens worldwide. Two decades into the 21st century, we must confront a troubling paradox: the same technologies that were heralded as democracy's saviors may be undermining its foundations.

Proponents of digital democracy highlight unprecedented access to information and platforms for civic engagement. Social media has enabled marginalized voices to reach global audiences, facilitated grassroots organizing, and increased transparency in governance. The Arab Spring, #MeToo movement, and numerous successful online petitions exemplify technology's potential to amplify citizen participation and challenge entrenched power structures.

However, these benefits come with significant costs that threaten democratic processes. Echo chambers and algorithmic filtering create information silos where citizens consume only content that reinforces existing beliefs, exacerbating polarization. The proliferation of misinformation—spreading six times faster than factual content on social platforms—erodes the shared factual basis necessary for democratic discourse. Furthermore, surveillance capitalism has commodified personal data, enabling unprecedented manipulation of public opinion through micro-targeted political advertising.

Perhaps most concerning is the concentration of communicative power in a handful of technology corporations. These entities now function as de facto public squares while operating under private, profit-driven imperatives. Their content moderation decisions—determining what speech is permissible—constitute governance without democratic accountability. When Facebook's user base exceeds the population of any single country, and its content policies affect global discourse more than many national laws, we must question whether democratic sovereignty has been quietly ceded to Silicon Valley.

Critics might argue that these concerns overstate technology's influence or underestimate citizens' agency. However, emerging research in cognitive psychology suggests that digital architectures exploit human vulnerabilities in attention and judgment, creating engagement through outrage and emotional triggering rather than reasoned deliberation—the cornerstone of democratic decision-making.

The solution is neither digital utopianism nor neo-Luddite rejection of technology. Rather, we need a recalibration of the relationship between technology and democracy through multifaceted approaches: algorithmic transparency requirements, digital literacy education, antitrust enforcement, and public alternatives to commercial platforms. Most fundamentally, we must recognize that technology is not neutral but embeds values and power relations that require democratic oversight.

The digital paradox demands that we move beyond simplistic narratives about technology's impact on democracy. The question is not whether digital tools will enhance or diminish democratic governance, but how we can design and govern these systems to serve democratic values rather than undermine them. Our answer will determine whether technology fulfills its emancipatory potential or accelerates democratic decline in the digital age.
Comprehension Questions:
What is the "digital paradox" referred to in the title?
What are two positive examples of technology enhancing democracy mentioned in the text?
How do echo chambers and algorithmic filtering affect democratic discourse?
What concern does the author raise about technology corporations?
What solutions does the author propose to address the problems identified?
What is the author's main argument about the relationship between technology and democracy?
✏️ Practice Exercises
📘 Practice 1 - Skimming and Main Idea Identification
Skim each paragraph below for 20 seconds, then identify the main idea without looking back at the text.

Climate change is altering global weather patterns, resulting in more frequent and severe extreme weather events. Rising temperatures have led to melting ice caps, rising sea levels, and changing precipitation patterns. These changes affect agriculture, water resources, and human settlements worldwide. Scientists project that without significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, these impacts will intensify in coming decades, threatening food security, coastal communities, and ecosystem stability.

Artificial intelligence has transformed numerous industries, from healthcare to transportation. Machine learning algorithms can now diagnose diseases, optimize traffic flow, and personalize educational content. However, these advancements raise ethical concerns about privacy, bias, and job displacement. As AI systems become more sophisticated, questions about transparency, accountability, and human oversight become increasingly important for policymakers and technologists alike.

The global shift toward remote work, accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, has fundamentally changed workplace dynamics. Organizations have adapted by implementing new communication tools, adjusting management practices, and reconsidering office space requirements. Employees report mixed experiences, with many appreciating increased flexibility and eliminated commutes, while others struggle with isolation and work-life boundaries. This transformation has implications for urban planning, commercial real estate, and labor policies worldwide.

Sustainable fashion addresses the environmental and ethical problems of the conventional fashion industry, which is one of the world's largest polluters. By using eco-friendly materials, reducing waste, ensuring fair labor practices, and designing for longevity rather than trends, sustainable fashion brands aim to minimize negative impacts. Consumers increasingly consider sustainability in purchasing decisions, driving industry change. However, truly sustainable fashion requires systemic transformation of production methods, business models, and consumption patterns.

📘 Practice 3 - Making Inferences
Read the following passages and answer the inference questions.
Passage 1:

Elena glanced at her watch and quickened her pace. The interview was in fifteen minutes, and she still had three blocks to walk. She adjusted her portfolio under her arm and silently cursed herself for not leaving earlier. As she waited at the crosswalk, she noticed a coffee stain on her white blouse. Perfect, she thought, just perfect. Her phone buzzed with a text: "Good luck today! You've got this!" She took a deep breath and straightened her shoulders as the light changed.
What is Elena going to do?
How is Elena feeling?
What time of day is it likely to be?
What can we infer about the person who sent the text?
Passage 2:

Professor Williams handed back the midterm exams with a grim expression. "The class average was a 62%," he announced. "I've never seen such poor results in my fifteen years of teaching this course." He paced at the front of the lecture hall. "Either this material is beyond your capabilities, or you're not putting in the necessary effort." Several students exchanged glances. Marcus stared at his paper, where a red 93% stood out at the top. He slowly slid the exam into his folder, avoiding eye contact with his classmates.
How did Marcus perform on the exam compared to his classmates?
How might Marcus be feeling?
What can we infer about Professor Williams' teaching style?
Why might Marcus be avoiding eye contact with his classmates?
📘 Practice 4 - Identifying Author's Purpose and Tone
Read each passage and identify the author's primary purpose (to inform, persuade, entertain, or instruct) and the tone (formal, informal, serious, humorous, critical, enthusiastic, etc.).
Passage 1:

The proposed tax increase would devastate small businesses already struggling to recover from the pandemic. Proponents claim it will fund essential services, but they conveniently ignore the job losses and business closures that will inevitably result. Haven't our local entrepreneurs suffered enough? It's time for citizens to speak out against this shortsighted proposal before it's too late. Contact your council representative today and demand they vote "no" on Proposition 37.
Passage 2:

To prepare this traditional dish, begin by soaking the beans overnight in cold water. The next day, drain and rinse thoroughly. In a large pot, sauté the diced onions and garlic in olive oil until translucent, approximately 5 minutes. Add the beans, bay leaves, and stock. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer uncovered for 90 minutes, stirring occasionally. The beans should be tender but not mushy. Season with salt and pepper in the final 15 minutes of cooking.
Passage 3:

Recent advances in quantum computing have significant implications for cryptography and data security. Unlike classical computers that use bits (0 or 1), quantum computers utilize qubits, which can exist in multiple states simultaneously due to the principle of superposition. This property enables quantum computers to solve certain complex problems exponentially faster than their classical counterparts. Particularly concerning is their theoretical ability to break widely used encryption algorithms, potentially compromising sensitive data protected by current security standards.
Passage 4:

So there I was, standing in the middle of the supermarket in my pajama pants and slippers, when I heard someone call my name. I froze, hoping against hope it wasn't anyone I knew. Slowly turning around, I came face to face with—you guessed it—my new boss. Of all the grocery stores in all the towns in all the world, she walks into mine, and on the one day I decide that bed-to-store is an acceptable fashion choice. The universe has a twisted sense of humor, doesn't it?
🔁 Deep Review
Effective reading in English requires mastering various strategies and understanding different text types. Here's a summary of key points:

Different reading purposes require different strategies: skimming for general ideas, scanning for specific information, intensive reading for detailed understanding, extensive reading for pleasure, and critical reading for evaluation
Text types include narrative, descriptive, expository, argumentative, and instructional, each with distinct features and requiring different approaches
Brazilian readers often face specific challenges: false cognates, phrasal verbs and idioms, complex sentence structures, unfamiliar cultural references, and different text organization patterns

Reading comprehension techniques include predicting content, identifying main ideas and supporting details, making inferences, recognizing author's purpose and tone, and summarizing/synthesizing information
Advanced readers should be able to understand explicit and implicit meanings, recognize bias and purpose, and critically evaluate what they read
Regular practice with diverse authentic materials is essential for developing versatile reading skills
Quick Review Questions:
What's the difference between skimming and scanning?
Name three common challenges Brazilian readers face when reading in English.
How can you identify an author's purpose in a text?
What strategies can help you understand complex academic texts?
🏠 Homework
📅 Day 1 - Writing

Choose one of the reading passages from the Practice Exercises section and write a summary (150-200 words). Then write a brief analysis (100-150 words) of the author's purpose, tone, and intended audience. Include specific examples from the text to support your analysis.
📅 Day 2 - Listening
Watch this TED Talk: "The destructive of a single story" by Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie (
https://www.ted.com/talks/chimamanda_ngozi_adichie_the_destructive_of_a_single_story
). As you listen, take notes on the main ideas and supporting examples. After watching, write a summary (200-250 words) of the talk and explain how it relates to critical reading skills.
📅 Day 3 - Grammar
Find a news article in English about a topic that interests you. Identify and list:
Five complex sentences (with multiple clauses)
Three examples of passive voice
Three instances of conditional structures
Five linking words/phrases that show relationships between ideas (however, therefore, in addition, etc.) For each item, explain how it contributes to the meaning and flow of the text.
📅 Day 4 - Speaking

Record yourself reading aloud one paragraph from each of the three reading practice texts in this lesson. Focus on pronunciation, intonation, and pacing. Then record yourself summarizing each text in your own words (1-2 minutes per text). Listen to your recordings and note areas for improvement.
📅 Day 5 - Vocabulary/Context
Create a personal "false friends" dictionary with at least 15 entries. For each entry, include:
The English word
The similar-looking Portuguese word
The actual meaning of the English word
The actual meaning of the Portuguese word
An example sentence using the English word correctly
A note about why this pair might cause confusion
📅 Day 6 - Creativity/Reflection
Choose one option:

Find an article or short text in Portuguese about your profession or a topic you're knowledgeable about. Translate it into English, paying attention to differences in text organization, sentence structure, and idiomatic expressions.
